title: Computer Vision with Convolutional Neural Networks
subtitle: Understand convolutions from the arithmetic up, build CNNs from LeNet to ResNet in PyTorch, and train, transfer and evaluate them for classification, detection and segmentation.
outcomes: Calculate convolution output sizes, parameter counts and receptive fields, and implement a convolution as a matrix multiplication
Build and compare CNNs from LeNet and VGG to ResNet and depthwise separable designs in PyTorch
Load image data with torchvision, and design augmentation that matches the shift between training and deployment images
Transfer pretrained networks to new classes by feature extraction and fine-tuning
Evaluate classifiers, detectors and segmenters with per-class metrics, calibration, mAP, IoU and Dice
prerequisites: Deep Learning with PyTorch, or equivalent experience writing PyTorch training loops with Dataset, DataLoader and nn.Module. Install Python 3.10 or later, PyTorch 2.6 or later and the matching torchvision (pip install torch torchvision, or the selector at pytorch.org; the CPU build is enough). All images are generated by the course's scripts, so nothing is downloaded except, optionally, ImageNet weights for ResNet-18 (about 45 MB) in the capstone.
description:
Convolutional neural networks are how machines read images, from phone apps that spot crop disease to systems that help doctors screen scans. This course takes them apart and rebuilds them in PyTorch and torchvision: what a convolution computes and how big its output is, why architectures moved from LeNet to VGG and ResNet, and how to make a network that does well on its test set also work on the images it will meet in the field.

You'll implement convolution as a matrix multiplication, measure what residual connections do to gradients, train on studio images and test on field images to see which augmentations close the gap, and transfer a pretrained network to new classes from a handful of labels. Then you'll score detections with average precision and train a small U-Net. Every image is generated on your own machine, so the labs run on a laptop CPU. The capstone asks a leaf disease classifier that has only seen studio photos to work in the field. The course builds on Deep Learning with PyTorch and goes further than the computer vision modules of Applied Machine Learning with TensorFlow.

modules.title: Convolutions from first principles
modules.summary: Turn images into tensors, then work out exactly what a convolution computes, how big its output is, how far each unit sees and what pooling adds.

lessons.title: Images as tensors
objectives: Convert images between PIL, NumPy and PyTorch layouts
Scale and normalise pixel values correctly
Batch images in the NCHW layout PyTorch expects
key_points: PyTorch's convolution layers expect float tensors in NCHW order: batch, channels, height, width. Images loaded with PIL or NumPy are height × width × channels with uint8 values from 0 to 255, so they need converting, with x.permute(2, 0, 1) for one image or with torchvision's transforms.

In torchvision.transforms.v2, ToImage() turns a PIL image or an HWC array into a CHW tensor, and ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True) maps 0-255 to floats from 0 to 1. The older ToTensor() did both at once and is deprecated in favour of this pair.

Normalize(mean, std) standardises each channel. Use the training set's statistics for a model trained from scratch, and the exact values a pretrained model was trained with when reusing it: mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and std [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] for torchvision's ImageNet models.

Colour images have three channels (RGB in PIL and torchvision; OpenCV loads BGR, a common source of silently wrong colours) and greyscale ones have one. A model's first convolution fixes the number of input channels, so give a greyscale image three channels before an RGB model sees it.

channels_last memory format, x.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last), keeps the logical NCHW shape but stores each pixel's channels next to each other, which many GPUs and CPUs process faster for convolutions; it's an optimisation that doesn't change your code's shapes.

lessons.title: The convolution operation
objectives: Explain what a convolutional layer computes, and the shape of its weights
Calculate output sizes from kernel size, stride, padding and dilation
Explain why convolutions need far fewer parameters than dense layers
key_points: A convolutional layer slides each filter over the input and, at every position, takes the dot product of the filter with the patch beneath it, plus a bias. Deep learning libraries compute cross-correlation (the kernel isn't flipped) and still call it convolution; for learned kernels the difference doesn't matter.

nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size) has a weight of shape (out_channels, in_channels, kH, kW): each filter spans every input channel and produces one output channel. It has out × in × kH × kW + out parameters, however large the image.

Along each dimension the output size is ⌊(n + 2p − d(k − 1) − 1) / s⌋ + 1 for input size n, kernel k, padding p, stride s and dilation d. With stride 1, padding (k − 1)/2 keeps the size for odd k, which padding='same' does for you (stride 1 only); stride 2 roughly halves it.

Sharing each filter across all positions, and connecting it only to a small patch, gives a convolution far fewer parameters than a dense layer, and makes it translation equivariant: shift the input and the output shifts by the same amount, away from the borders.

Zero padding makes the borders look like edges, as a filter sees a jump from the image to zeros; padding_mode='reflect' or 'replicate' avoids that where it matters. Dilation spaces a kernel's taps apart, widening its view without adding weights.

F.unfold extracts every patch as a column (im2col), after which a convolution is a single matrix multiplication of the flattened filters by the columns: one classic way to compute convolutions quickly.

lessons.title: Receptive fields, pooling and invariance
objectives: Calculate the receptive field of a unit in a stack of layers
Downsample with max pooling, average pooling and strided convolutions
Distinguish translation equivariance from invariance
key_points: A unit's receptive field is the patch of input pixels that can affect it. Each layer adds (k − 1) × j pixels, where j is the product of the strides before it, so three stacked 3×3 convolutions see 7×7 pixels, and after downsampling the field grows much faster.

nn.MaxPool2d(2) keeps the largest value in each 2×2 window and halves the height and width; average pooling takes the mean. Pooling has no parameters and acts on each channel separately; a convolution with stride 2 is a learned alternative that many modern networks use.

Global average pooling, nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), averages each channel over the whole feature map, giving one number per channel whatever the input size. Followed by one Linear layer, it replaces large flattened classifier heads and makes the output nearly independent of where the object is.

Convolutions are translation equivariant (shift the input and the feature maps shift); pooling and global averaging add some translation invariance (the output hardly changes). Neither gives invariance to rotation, scale or lighting: a network learns those only from data that shows them, or from augmentation.

Visualised first-layer filters of trained CNNs typically look like oriented edge and colour detectors, and deeper layers respond to textures, parts and whole objects: a hierarchy that makes features learned on one dataset reusable on another.

"""Convolution by hand: output sizes, im2col with unfold, parameter counts, receptive fields and an edge filter."""

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn


def out_size(n, k, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1):
    """Output length along one spatial dimension of a convolution (or pooling) layer."""
    # TODO: return floor((n + 2*padding - dilation*(k - 1) - 1) / stride) + 1, using integer division
    return n


def conv2d_loops(x, weight, bias):
    """The definition, for stride 1 and no padding: slide each filter over every position (cross-correlation)."""
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    c_out, _, k, _ = weight.shape
    out = torch.zeros(n, c_out, h - k + 1, w - k + 1)
    for i in range(h - k + 1):
        for j in range(w - k + 1):
            patch = x[:, :, i:i + k, j:j + k]                       # (N, C, k, k)
            out[:, :, i, j] = (patch.unsqueeze(1) * weight).sum(dim=(2, 3, 4)) + bias
    return out


def conv2d_unfold(x, weight, bias, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1):
    """The same result as F.conv2d, computed as one matrix multiplication (im2col)."""
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    c_out, _, kh, kw = weight.shape
    cols = F.unfold(x, (kh, kw), dilation=dilation, padding=padding, stride=stride)   # (N, C*kh*kw, positions)
    # TODO: multiply the weights flattened to (c_out, C*kh*kw) by cols, add the bias (shaped (1, c_out, 1)),
    #  and reshape to (N, c_out, H_out, W_out) using out_size() for each dimension
    return torch.zeros(n, c_out, 1, 1)


def receptive_field(layers):
    """layers: (kernel, stride) pairs, input first. Returns the receptive field of one output unit, in pixels."""
    r, jump = 1, 1
    for k, s in layers:
        # TODO: each layer widens the field by (k - 1) * jump, then multiplies the jump by its stride
        pass
    return r


def n_params(module):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in module.parameters())


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    x = torch.randn(2, 3, 11, 13)
    conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 4, 3)
    print("== 1. Definition, im2col and F.conv2d agree")
    loops = conv2d_loops(x, conv.weight.detach(), conv.bias.detach())
    print(f"loops vs F.conv2d: max |diff| {(loops - conv(x)).abs().max().item():.1e}, shape {tuple(loops.shape)}")
    for stride, padding, dilation in [(1, 0, 1), (2, 1, 1), (1, 2, 2), (3, 1, 1)]:
        ref = F.conv2d(x, conv.weight, conv.bias, stride=stride, padding=padding, dilation=dilation)
        mine = conv2d_unfold(x, conv.weight, conv.bias, stride, padding, dilation)
        ok = mine.shape == ref.shape and torch.allclose(mine, ref, atol=1e-5)
        print(f"stride {stride} padding {padding} dilation {dilation}: {tuple(ref.shape)} "
              f"formula {out_size(11, 3, stride, padding, dilation)} x {out_size(13, 3, stride, padding, dilation)} "
              f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}")

    print("== 2. Parameters")
    std = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1)
    separable = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(32, 32, 3, padding=1, groups=32), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 1))
    print(f"Conv2d(3, 16, 5): {n_params(nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 5))}  (16 x 3 x 5 x 5 + 16)")
    print(f"standard 3x3, 32 -> 64: {n_params(std)}; depthwise separable: {n_params(separable)}; "
          f"same output shape: {std(torch.randn(1, 32, 8, 8)).shape == separable(torch.randn(1, 32, 8, 8)).shape}")
    two_3x3, one_5x5 = 2 * 9 * 64 * 64, 25 * 64 * 64
    print(f"two 3x3 layers vs one 5x5 (64 channels, no bias): {two_3x3} vs {one_5x5} weights")

    print("== 3. Receptive fields")
    print("three 3x3 convs, stride 1:", receptive_field([(3, 1)] * 3))
    print("LeNet-style conv5, pool2, conv5, pool2:", receptive_field([(5, 1), (2, 2), (5, 1), (2, 2)]))
    print("ResNet stem conv7/2 + pool3/2, then four 3x3:", receptive_field([(7, 2), (3, 2)] + [(3, 1)] * 4))

    print("== 4. An edge filter")
    img = torch.zeros(1, 1, 6, 8)
    img[..., 4:] = 1.0                                              # dark left, bright right
    sobel_x = torch.tensor([[-1.0, 0.0, 1.0], [-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]]).view(1, 1, 3, 3)
    edges = F.conv2d(img, sobel_x, padding=1)
    print("row 2 of the image: ", img[0, 0, 2].int().tolist())
    print("row 2 of the response:", edges[0, 0, 2].int().tolist())
    moved = torch.zeros_like(img)
    moved[..., 5:] = 1.0                                            # the same edge, one pixel to the right
    shifted = F.conv2d(moved, sobel_x, padding=1)
    print("move the edge one pixel right, and the response moves with it:",
          torch.equal(shifted[0, 0, 2, 1:7], edges[0, 0, 2, 0:6]))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: CNN architectures from LeNet to ResNet
modules.summary: Follow the ideas that made CNNs deeper and better, from LeNet's conv-pool pattern through VGG and Inception to residual networks and depthwise separable convolutions, and build each in PyTorch.

lessons.title: LeNet and the classic CNN pattern
objectives: Describe LeNet-5's convolution, pooling and dense layers
Build a LeNet-style network and size its flattened layer
Compare flattened heads with global average pooling
key_points: LeNet-5 (LeCun and colleagues, 1998) read handwritten digits from 32×32 greyscale images with two 5×5 convolution layers of 6 and 16 filters, each followed by subsampling, then fully connected layers of 120 and 84 units and 10 outputs: the conv-pool-dense pattern later CNNs refined.

nn.Flatten() turns each (C, H, W) feature map into a vector of C × H × W values, so the first Linear layer's in_features depends on the input size: work it out with the output-size formula, pass a dummy batch through the convolutional part, or use nn.LazyLinear, which infers it on the first forward pass.

A flattened head gives every weight a fixed position, so it must learn each pattern separately at each place and only accepts one input size. Global average pooling followed by one Linear layer has far fewer parameters and accepts any input size.
Modern versions of the pattern use ReLU instead of tanh, max pooling instead of LeNet's averaging subsampling, and batch normalisation after each convolution.

lessons.title: AlexNet, VGG and Inception: depth, small kernels and 1×1 convolutions
objectives: Explain what AlexNet, VGG and Inception each contributed
Compare stacked small kernels with one large kernel
Use 1×1 convolutions and batch normalisation in CNNs
key_points: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet challenge by a wide margin with five convolutional and three fully connected layers trained on GPUs, using ReLU activations, dropout in the dense layers and data augmentation, and started the deep learning era in computer vision.

VGG networks (2014) used only 3×3 convolutions, two to four at a time between poolings, to reach 16 and 19 layers. Two 3×3 layers see as far as one 5×5 with 18 weights per channel pair instead of 25, and an extra non-linearity. VGG-16 has about 138 million parameters, most in its dense layers.

A 1×1 convolution mixes channels at each pixel without looking at its neighbours, like a dense layer applied per pixel. Inception (GoogLeNet, 2014) ran 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions and pooling in parallel branches, with 1×1 bottleneck layers reducing the channels first to keep the cost down.

nn.BatchNorm2d normalises each channel over the batch and every spatial position (N × H × W values per channel), with a learned scale and shift per channel. Placed after a convolution, which then needs no bias, it let much deeper networks train with higher learning rates.

lessons.title: Residual networks
objectives: Explain the degradation problem that residual connections solve
Build basic residual blocks with identity and projection shortcuts
Read the structure of torchvision's ResNets
key_points: Stacking more layers eventually makes a plain network worse even on its training data: deeper plain networks reached higher training error than shallower ones. This degradation isn't overfitting but an optimisation problem, and residual networks (He and colleagues, 2015) were designed to fix it.

A residual block computes y = F(x) + x: its layers learn a correction F to their input, which a shortcut adds back. If the best mapping is close to the identity, F only needs to be near zero, and the shortcut gives gradients a direct path to earlier layers, keeping their sizes more even through depth.

When a block changes the number of channels or the resolution, the shortcut becomes a projection, usually a 1×1 convolution with stride 2 and batch norm, so the shapes match for the addition. ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 use basic blocks of two 3×3 convolutions; ResNet-50 and deeper use bottleneck blocks (1×1, 3×3, 1×1).

torchvision's ResNets start with a 7×7 stride-2 convolution and a stride-2 max pool, then four stages of 64, 128, 256 and 512 channels (times 4 with bottleneck blocks), halving the resolution at stages 2-4, and end with global average pooling and one Linear layer. resnet18 has about 11.7 million parameters.

lessons.title: Efficient convolutions
objectives: Compute the savings of depthwise separable convolutions
Use the groups argument of nn.Conv2d
Name the efficient and modern alternatives to ResNet backbones
key_points: A depthwise convolution (groups = in_channels) filters each channel on its own, and a pointwise 1×1 convolution then mixes the channels. Together they need k² × C_in + C_in × C_out weights instead of k² × C_in × C_out: for 3×3 kernels from 32 to 64 channels, 2,432 parameters instead of 18,496, biases included.

groups=g in nn.Conv2d splits the input and output channels into g groups and convolves each group separately, dividing the weights by g; groups = in_channels is the depthwise case. Both in_channels and out_channels must be divisible by groups.

MobileNets build on depthwise separable convolutions to run on phones; MobileNetV2 adds inverted residual blocks, and EfficientNet scales depth, width and resolution together. Squeeze-and-excitation blocks reweight each channel using globally pooled statistics.

Fewer parameters and multiply-adds don't always mean faster: depthwise convolutions do little arithmetic for each byte they move, so measure speed on the target device. ConvNeXt (2022) and vision transformers are the main modern alternatives to ResNet-style backbones.

"""Build LeNet, a VGG-style network and a ResNet, compare their sizes and shapes, and see what residual connections do."""

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from torchvision.models import resnet18

from shapes import make_shapes


class LeNet(nn.Module):
    """LeNet-5's layout for 32 x 32 RGB images, with ReLU and max pooling instead of tanh and subsampling."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, 6, 5), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),      # 32 -> 28 -> 14
                                      nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))     # 14 -> 10 -> 5
        # TODO: the classifier: nn.Flatten(), then Linear layers 16*5*5 -> 120 -> 84 -> n_classes with ReLU between
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.LazyLinear(n_classes))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.classifier(self.features(x))


def vgg_stage(c_in, c_out):
    """Two 3x3 convolutions with batch norm and ReLU, then 2x2 max pooling."""
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU(),
                         nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU(),
                         nn.MaxPool2d(2))


def small_vgg(n_classes=3):
    return nn.Sequential(vgg_stage(3, 32), vgg_stage(32, 64), vgg_stage(64, 128),
                         nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(128, n_classes))


class BasicBlock(nn.Module):
    """Two 3x3 convolutions; with residual=True their output is added to a shortcut from the input."""

    def __init__(self, c_in, c_out, stride=1, residual=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.residual = residual
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out)
        self.shortcut = nn.Identity()
        if stride != 1 or c_in != c_out:            # a projection, so the shapes match for the addition
            self.shortcut = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 1, stride=stride, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out))

    def forward(self, x):
        out = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        # TODO: if self.residual, add self.shortcut(x) to out; then return the ReLU of the result
        return F.relu(out)


def small_resnet(n_classes=3):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, 16, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(),
                         BasicBlock(16, 16), BasicBlock(16, 32, stride=2), BasicBlock(32, 64, stride=2),
                         nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64, n_classes))


def deep_net(residual, blocks=15, width=16):
    """A 32-layer network: a stem, 15 blocks of two convolutions, and a linear classifier."""
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, width, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(width), nn.ReLU(),
                         *[BasicBlock(width, width, residual=residual) for _ in range(blocks)],
                         nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(width, 3))


def n_params(model):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    print("== 1. Size")
    for name, model in [("LeNet", LeNet()), ("small VGG", small_vgg()), ("small ResNet", small_resnet()),
                        ("torchvision resnet18", resnet18(weights=None))]:
        print(f"{name:22} {n_params(model):>10,} parameters")

    print("== 2. Shapes through torchvision's ResNet-18 (one 224 x 224 image)")
    net = resnet18(weights=None).eval()
    x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for name, layer in net.named_children():
            x = torch.flatten(x, 1) if name == "fc" else x
            x = layer(x)
            if name in ("conv1", "maxpool", "layer1", "layer2", "layer3", "layer4", "avgpool", "fc"):
                print(f"after {name:8} {tuple(x.shape)}")

    print("== 3. Gradients at initialisation, 32 layers deep")
    data = make_shapes(2000, seed=0)
    val = make_shapes(500, seed=1)
    for residual in (False, True):
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = deep_net(residual)
        F.cross_entropy(model(data["images"][:128]), data["labels"][:128]).backward()
        first = model[0].weight.grad.norm().item()
        last = model[-4].conv2.weight.grad.norm().item()
        print(f"{'residual' if residual else 'plain':9} first conv {first:.2e}  last block {last:.2e}  "
              f"ratio {first / last:.1f}")

    print("== 4. Training the two 32-layer networks for 3 epochs")
    loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(data["images"], data["labels"]), batch_size=64, shuffle=True,
                        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
    for residual in (False, True):
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = deep_net(residual)
        optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
        scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(optimizer, 3e-3, epochs=3, steps_per_epoch=len(loader))
        for epoch in range(1, 4):
            model.train()
            total, n = 0.0, 0
            for X, y in loader:
                optimizer.zero_grad()
                loss = F.cross_entropy(model(X), y)
                loss.backward()
                optimizer.step()
                scheduler.step()
                total, n = total + loss.item() * len(y), n + len(y)
            model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                acc = (model(val["images"]).argmax(1) == val["labels"]).float().mean().item()
            print(f"{'residual' if residual else 'plain':9} epoch {epoch}  train loss {total / n:.3f}  val acc {acc:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: A shape error in LeNet's first Linear layer means in_features doesn't match 16 * 5 * 5; print the shape after self.features to check.
The shortcut is nn.Identity() when the shapes already match, and a 1 x 1 convolution with batch norm when they don't, so self.shortcut(x) always has the same shape as out.

modules.title: Training CNNs: data, augmentation and shift
modules.summary: Load image datasets without leaking between splits, augment them with torchvision's v2 transforms, and find out how a model trained on tidy images copes with the ones it will really meet.

lessons.title: Image datasets and loaders
objectives: Load a folder of labelled images with ImageFolder
Give each split its own transforms
Split image data by group, and handle imbalanced classes
key_points: torchvision.datasets.ImageFolder reads a folder with one subfolder per class (root/healthy/001.png). It sorts the subfolder names to assign labels (case-sensitively, so 'Mosaic' comes before 'blight'), lists them in .classes and .class_to_idx, and returns PIL images unless you pass a transform.

Give training, validation and test data different transforms, with random augmentation only for training. Subsets from random_split share their dataset's transform, so build a separate dataset for each split over the same files, or wrap the subsets in a Dataset that applies its own transform.

Split by the unit you need to generalise to: when one patient, plant, camera or session gives many images, keep all of them in the same split, for example with scikit-learn's GroupShuffleSplit. Near-duplicate images across splits inflate the test score without anyone noticing.

For imbalanced classes, weight the loss with CrossEntropyLoss(weight=...) or oversample rare classes with WeightedRandomSampler(weights, num_samples, replacement=True), which replaces shuffle=True in the DataLoader, and report per-class metrics, not only accuracy.

Decoding and resizing images can limit training speed more than the model does: use num_workers > 0, store images near the training resolution, and watch processor use during training to find the bottleneck.

lessons.title: Data augmentation with torchvision transforms
objectives: Build augmentation pipelines with torchvision.transforms.v2
Choose augmentations that keep labels true
Augment boxes and masks with their images, and mix batches with MixUp and CutMix
key_points: Augmentation applies random, label-preserving changes to each training image every time it's loaded, so each epoch sees a different version. It teaches invariances the data doesn't show enough of, such as position, scale, rotation and lighting, and acts as a strong regulariser.

torchvision.transforms.v2 offers geometric transforms (RandomResizedCrop, RandomHorizontalFlip, RandomRotation, RandomAffine), photometric ones (ColorJitter, GaussianBlur, GaussianNoise) and RandomErasing, chained with v2.Compose. Apply them per image in the Dataset: on a batch tensor a v2 transform uses one set of random parameters for all.

Use only augmentations that keep the label true: a horizontal flip suits most photographs but not digits or text (a mirrored 2 isn't a 2), and a 180° rotation turns a 6 into a 9. Strong augmentation makes training harder, so it often needs more epochs to pay off.

v2 transforms change bounding boxes, masks and keypoints together with the image when they're wrapped as tv_tensors (BoundingBoxes, Mask, KeyPoints), so a flip or crop moves the boxes too, which detection and segmentation need.

MixUp blends pairs of images and their labels; CutMix pastes a patch of one image into another and mixes the labels by area. v2.MixUp and v2.CutMix act on a whole batch after the DataLoader and return soft labels, which CrossEntropyLoss accepts as class probabilities.

lessons.title: When test images don't look like training images
objectives: Recognise domain shift between training and deployment images
Build test sets and breakdowns that reveal it
Judge what augmentation can and can't fix
key_points: A model is only as good as the match between its training images and the ones it will meet: a classifier trained on studio photos (centred, well lit, plain backgrounds) can score close to 100% on studio test images and far less on photos taken in the field.

Build a test set that looks like deployment, from the same cameras, places and conditions, and report it separately from an in-distribution test set: the gap between the two measures what the shift costs.

Augmentation can close part of the gap when the shift is in factors you can simulate, such as position, scale, tilt, brightness, contrast and noise, but only if it simulates each of them; it can't create what the training images lack, such as new backgrounds or new kinds of lesion. Then you need new data.

Break results down by condition, such as lighting, background, device or site: an average can hide a condition where the model fails, and in medical imaging such failures can fall on particular hospitals or groups of patients.

Test-time augmentation averages a model's predictions over several augmented copies of each test image, such as flips and crops, which often improves accuracy and calibration a little at the cost of extra forward passes.

"""Train on studio images, test in the field: which augmentations close the gap?

python augment.py --aug none | geometric | photometric | both
Trains the same CNN for 15 epochs on 2,000 studio images of circles, squares and triangles, then reports its
accuracy on studio test images and on field images, broken down by background and shape size.
"""

import argparse

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Dataset
from torchvision.transforms import v2

from shapes import make_shapes


class ShapesDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, data, transform=None):
        self.images, self.labels, self.transform = data["images"], data["labels"], transform

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.labels)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        # TODO: apply self.transform (if there is one) to image i, clamp the result to [0, 1], and return it
        #  with the label. Transforming here, one image at a time, gives each image its own random parameters
        return self.images[i], self.labels[i]


def pipelines():
    # TODO: geometric: v2.RandomAffine with degrees=30, translate=(0.2, 0.2), scale=(0.7, 1.25) and fill=0.75
    #  (a light grey like the studio backgrounds, rather than black corners).
    #  photometric: v2.Compose of v2.RandomInvert(p=0.5), v2.ColorJitter(brightness=(0.4, 1.2), contrast=0.4,
    #  saturation=0.5, hue=0.5) and v2.GaussianNoise(sigma=0.06)
    geometric = photometric = None
    return {"none": None, "geometric": geometric, "photometric": photometric,
            "both": v2.Compose([geometric, photometric]) if geometric else None}


def cnn():
    def conv(c_in, c_out):
        return [nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU()]
    return nn.Sequential(*conv(3, 32), *conv(32, 32), nn.MaxPool2d(2), *conv(32, 64), *conv(64, 64), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                         *conv(64, 128), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(128, 3))


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--aug", default="none", choices=["none", "geometric", "photometric", "both"])
    parser.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=15)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    train, studio, field = make_shapes(2000, seed=0), make_shapes(500, seed=1), make_shapes(500, seed=2, setting="field")

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = cnn()
    loader = DataLoader(ShapesDataset(train, pipelines()[args.aug]), batch_size=64, shuffle=True,
                        generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(optimizer, 3e-3, epochs=args.epochs, steps_per_epoch=len(loader))
    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        model.train()
        correct = seen = 0
        for X, y in loader:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            logits = model(X)
            F.cross_entropy(logits, y).backward()
            optimizer.step()
            scheduler.step()
            correct, seen = correct + (logits.argmax(1) == y).sum().item(), seen + len(y)

    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        studio_ok = (model(studio["images"]).argmax(1) == studio["labels"]).float()
        field_ok = (model(field["images"]).argmax(1) == field["labels"]).float()
    dark = field["images"][:, :, :3, :3].mean(dim=(1, 2, 3)) < 0.3          # judged from a corner of the image
    small = (field["boxes"][:, 2] - field["boxes"][:, 0]) < 14
    print(f"aug={args.aug:11} train acc (last epoch, augmented) {correct / seen:.3f} | studio {studio_ok.mean():.3f} | "
          f"field {field_ok.mean():.3f}")
    print(f"   field by condition: dark background {field_ok[dark].mean():.3f}, light {field_ok[~dark].mean():.3f}; "
          f"small shapes {field_ok[small].mean():.3f}, large {field_ok[~small].mean():.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Don't apply the transform to the whole batch after the DataLoader: v2 transforms draw one set of random parameters per call, so every image in the batch would get the same flip and the same rotation.
fill=0.75 paints the corners that rotation and translation uncover in light grey, like the studio backgrounds; the default fill of 0 would add black corners that no real image has.
Strong augmentation makes the training set harder: a lower training accuracy with augmentation is expected.

modules.title: Transfer learning
modules.summary: Reuse networks pretrained on large datasets: load them and their preprocessing from torchvision, then adapt them by feature extraction or fine-tuning, and avoid the ways transfer goes wrong.

lessons.title: Pretrained models in torchvision
objectives: Explain why features learned on one dataset help on another
Load torchvision models with or without pretrained weights
Apply the preprocessing a pretrained model expects
key_points: Transfer learning starts a new task from a network trained on a large dataset, usually ImageNet's 1.28 million training images in 1,000 classes. Its early layers detect generic edges, colours and textures, so a task with little data can start from good features instead of random ones.

torchvision's builders take a weights argument: resnet18(weights=ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT) downloads the best available weights on first use and caches them under ~/.cache/torch/hub, while weights=None builds the same architecture with random weights and downloads nothing.

Each weights enum carries its preprocessing and metadata: weights.transforms() returns the resize, crop and normalisation the model expects (for ResNet-18: resize to 256, centre-crop to 224, ImageNet mean and standard deviation) and weights.meta['categories'] lists the classes.

The pretrained=True argument of older tutorials has been deprecated since torchvision 0.13 in favour of weights=. Other sources of pretrained models include timm and the Hugging Face Hub; check each model's licence and training data before using it in a product, and record exactly which weights you started from.

lessons.title: Feature extraction and fine-tuning
objectives: Replace a pretrained model's head for new classes
Train a linear probe on a frozen backbone
Fine-tune with parameter groups and smaller learning rates
key_points: To adapt a pretrained classifier, replace its last layer with one for your classes: model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, n_classes) for torchvision's ResNets; other families name it differently, such as the last layer of model.classifier for MobileNet and EfficientNet, or model.heads for vision transformers.

Feature extraction, or a linear probe, freezes the backbone with requires_grad_(False) and trains only the new head: quick, and hard to overfit with very few labels. Give the optimiser only the trainable parameters.

Keep a frozen backbone in evaluation mode: model.train() switches every submodule to training mode, so its batch-norm layers would keep updating their running statistics from your small batches. Call .eval() on the backbone after model.train(), or compute its features once and train the head on them.

Fine-tuning trains the whole network, usually with a smaller learning rate for the pretrained layers than for the new head (two parameter groups, often about 10 times apart), so the features adapt without being wiped out. Unfreezing the last stage first and more later is a common compromise.

A linear probe is the cheapest, safest start with very few labels; fine-tuning with a small backbone learning rate usually does better as labels grow, and sometimes even with few, as in this module's lab. The further your images are from the pretraining data, the more of the network has to adapt.

lessons.title: When transfer goes wrong
objectives: Recognise preprocessing mismatches and catastrophic forgetting
Detect negative transfer with a from-scratch baseline
Evaluate fairly when the labelled data is tiny
key_points: Preprocessing must match: feed a pretrained model images normalised with its own mean and standard deviation, at about the resolution it was trained at. Forgetting the normalisation, or passing BGR images to an RGB model, silently weakens its features.
A learning rate meant for training from scratch can wreck pretrained features within a few steps (catastrophic forgetting). Train the new head first, or give the backbone a much smaller rate.

Negative transfer happens when the source task's features don't suit the target, for example features from too narrow a task: a pretrained start can then do worse than training from scratch. Always compare against a from-scratch baseline on the same data.
With tiny datasets, a few validation images give a very noisy estimate: use cross-validation or repeated splits, report the spread, and keep a final test set you look at once.

"""Transfer learning without downloads: pretrain a CNN on six shape classes, then reuse it for three new ones.

The first run pretrains the source model on 6,000 field images (a few minutes on a laptop CPU) and saves it to
source_cnn.pt; later runs load it. Then, for 5, 20 and 50 labelled images per new class, it compares training from
scratch, a frozen pretrained backbone with a new head (a linear probe), and fine-tuning the whole network.
"""

import copy
import os

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn

from shapes import make_shapes

SOURCE = ["circle", "ring", "square", "triangle", "cross", "crescent"]
TARGET = ["star", "l_shape", "t_shape"]


def cnn(n_classes):
    def conv(c_in, c_out):
        return [nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU()]
    backbone = nn.Sequential(*conv(3, 32), *conv(32, 32), nn.MaxPool2d(2), *conv(32, 64), *conv(64, 64),
                             nn.MaxPool2d(2), *conv(64, 128), nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten())
    return nn.Sequential(backbone, nn.Linear(128, n_classes))      # model[0] is the backbone, model[1] the head


def accuracy(model, data):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (model(data["images"]).argmax(1) == data["labels"]).float().mean().item()


def fit(model, param_groups, data, epochs, batch_size=16, frozen_backbone=False):
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(param_groups)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    X, y = data["images"], data["labels"]
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        if frozen_backbone:
            model[0].eval()          # keep the backbone's batch-norm statistics as they were
        order = torch.randperm(len(y), generator=g)
        for start in range(0, len(y), batch_size):
            idx = order[start:start + batch_size]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            F.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx]).backward()
            optimizer.step()
    return model


def pretrained_source():
    if os.path.exists("source_cnn.pt"):
        model = cnn(len(SOURCE))
        model.load_state_dict(torch.load("source_cnn.pt"))
        return model
    print("pretraining on 6,000 images of", ", ".join(SOURCE), "...")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    model = cnn(len(SOURCE))
    fit(model, [{"params": model.parameters(), "lr": 3e-3}], make_shapes(6000, SOURCE, seed=10, setting="field"),
        epochs=8, batch_size=64)
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), "source_cnn.pt")
    return model


def frozen_probe(source):
    model = copy.deepcopy(source)
    # TODO: give the copy a new head, nn.Linear(128, len(TARGET)); freeze every parameter of the backbone
    #  (model[0].requires_grad_(False)); return the model and the parameter groups for the optimiser: only the
    #  head's parameters, with lr 1e-2
    return model, [{"params": model.parameters(), "lr": 1e-2}]


def fine_tune(source):
    model = copy.deepcopy(source)
    # TODO: give the copy a new head as above, keep everything trainable, and return two parameter groups:
    #  the backbone at lr 3e-4 and the head at lr 3e-3
    return model, [{"params": model.parameters(), "lr": 3e-3}]


def trainable(model):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)


def main():
    source = pretrained_source()
    print(f"source model: {accuracy(source, make_shapes(600, SOURCE, seed=11, setting='field')):.3f} accuracy "
          f"on new images of its own six classes")
    pool = make_shapes(600, TARGET, seed=20, setting="field")
    test = make_shapes(900, TARGET, seed=21, setting="field")
    print(f"{'labelled per class':>18} | {'scratch':>8} | {'frozen backbone':>15} | {'fine-tuned':>10}")
    for k in (5, 20, 50):
        idx = torch.cat([torch.nonzero(pool["labels"] == c).flatten()[:k] for c in range(len(TARGET))])
        few = {"images": pool["images"][idx], "labels": pool["labels"][idx]}
        epochs = max(30, 3000 // len(idx))          # roughly the same number of updates for every k
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        scratch = cnn(len(TARGET))
        fit(scratch, [{"params": scratch.parameters(), "lr": 3e-3}], few, epochs)
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        probe, groups = frozen_probe(source)
        fit(probe, groups, few, epochs, frozen_backbone=True)
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        tuned, groups = fine_tune(source)
        fit(tuned, groups, few, epochs)
        print(f"{k:>18} | {accuracy(scratch, test):8.3f} | {accuracy(probe, test):15.3f} | {accuracy(tuned, test):10.3f}")
    print(f"trainable parameters: scratch {trainable(scratch):,}, frozen backbone {trainable(probe):,}, "
          f"fine-tuned {trainable(tuned):,}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.summary: Evaluate classifiers beyond accuracy, then move from labelling images to locating and outlining what's in them: detectors and their mAP, and segmenters with IoU and Dice.

lessons.title: Evaluating image classifiers
objectives: Read confusion matrices and per-class metrics
Measure calibration and fix it with temperature scaling
Analyse errors by example and by subgroup
key_points: Accuracy hides which classes fail: read the confusion matrix (rows are true classes and columns predictions, in scikit-learn's convention) with per-class precision and recall, and use the macro average when every class matters equally, however rare.

Softmax outputs are often over-confident. Calibration compares confidence with accuracy: put predictions into confidence bins, and the expected calibration error (ECE) is the average gap between each bin's mean confidence and its accuracy, weighted by the share of predictions in it.

Temperature scaling divides the logits by one number T, fitted on validation data to minimise the cross-entropy. T above 1 softens over-confident predictions, and because it never changes which class scores highest, accuracy stays exactly the same.
Look at the errors, especially confident ones: they reveal label mistakes, ambiguous images and shortcuts, such as a model that learned the background or a ruler in the photo instead of the object.
Report results by subgroup and condition, such as camera, site, lighting or skin tone in medical images: a model can be accurate on average and unreliable for a group that matters.

walkthrough.title: Measure calibration, then fix it with a temperature

steps.do: Simulate an over-confident classifier's logits and compute its expected calibration error (ECE).
steps.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)
labels = torch.randint(0, 4, (2000,))
logits = torch.randn(2000, 4)
logits[torch.arange(2000), labels] += 1.5    # some signal
logits *= 3                                  # and far too much confidence

def ece(logits, labels, bins=10):
    conf, pred = F.softmax(logits, dim=1).max(dim=1)
    edges = torch.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)
    total = 0.0
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        inside = (conf > lo) & (conf <= hi)
        if inside.any():
            gap = (pred[inside] == labels[inside]).float().mean() - conf[inside].mean()
            total += inside.float().mean() * gap.abs()
    return float(total)

conf = F.softmax(logits, 1).max(1).values.mean().item()
acc = (logits.argmax(1) == labels).float().mean().item()
print(f"mean confidence {conf:.3f}, accuracy {acc:.3f}, ECE {ece(logits, labels):.3f}")
steps.see: mean confidence 0.836, accuracy 0.697, ECE 0.140: far more confident than accurate.

steps.do: Fit a temperature by minimising the cross-entropy of logits / T (in practice on validation logits, then checked on the test set), and compare.
steps.code:
log_t = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([log_t], lr=0.1, max_iter=100)

def closure():
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits / log_t.exp(), labels)
    loss.backward()
    return loss

opt.step(closure)
T = log_t.exp().item()
scaled = logits / T
print(f"T = {T:.2f}; accuracy {(scaled.argmax(1) == labels).float().mean().item():.3f}; ECE {ece(scaled, labels):.3f}")
steps.see: T = 1.96; accuracy 0.697; ECE 0.011: the same accuracy, and a much smaller calibration error.

lessons.title: Object detection
objectives: Handle box formats correctly
Compare two-stage, one-stage, anchor-free and transformer detectors
Use torchvision's detection models and their inputs and outputs
key_points: A detector outputs a box, a class and a confidence score for each object. Boxes come as (x1, y1, x2, y2) corners, as torchvision uses; (x, y, w, h), as COCO's annotation files use; or (cx, cy, w, h) centres. torchvision.ops.box_convert converts between them, and mixing them up is a classic bug.

IoU measures how much two boxes overlap and non-maximum suppression removes duplicate detections of one object (both covered in Applied Machine Learning with TensorFlow); in PyTorch, torchvision.ops.box_iou and torchvision.ops.nms implement them.

Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN propose candidate regions with a region proposal network, then classify each one and refine its box; one-stage detectors such as SSD, RetinaNet and the YOLO family predict classes and boxes densely in one pass. RetinaNet's focal loss down-weights the many easy background examples.

Many detectors predict offsets from preset anchor boxes at each position; anchor-free ones such as FCOS predict boxes directly from points. DETR treats detection as set prediction with a transformer, matching predictions to objects one-to-one with the Hungarian algorithm, so it needs no non-maximum suppression.

torchvision's detection models, such as fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2, take a list of image tensors and, in training mode, a list of target dicts with 'boxes' and 'labels', returning a dict of losses; in evaluation mode they return one dict per image with 'boxes', 'labels' and 'scores'.

lessons.title: Measuring detectors: precision, recall and mAP
objectives: Match detections to ground truth at an IoU threshold
Compute average precision from a precision-recall curve
Interpret AP50, COCO's mAP and their limits
key_points: To score a detector, sort its detections by confidence and match each one to the unmatched ground-truth box of its class with the highest IoU, if that IoU reaches a threshold such as 0.5. Matches are true positives, other detections false positives, and unmatched ground truths misses.

Precision and recall after each detection, in that order, trace the precision-recall curve. Average precision (AP) is the area under it once precision is made non-increasing, each point taking the highest precision found at any equal or higher recall.

mAP averages AP over classes. Pascal VOC reports AP at IoU 0.5 (AP50); COCO's main metric averages AP over ten IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, sampling the curve at 101 recall points, which rewards precise boxes. COCO also reports AP for small, medium and large objects.

AP summarises every confidence threshold at once, so choose the threshold you'll deploy with separately, from the precision and recall you need, and break the errors down: missed objects, duplicates, poorly placed boxes and confusions between classes.

lessons.title: Semantic and instance segmentation
objectives: Distinguish semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation
Build an encoder-decoder with skip connections
Choose segmentation losses and metrics that suit the data
key_points: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class; instance segmentation also separates individual objects of the same class; panoptic segmentation does both. A segmentation network outputs logits of shape (N, C, H, W), which nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes with integer targets of shape (N, H, W).

Encoder-decoder networks downsample to gather context, then upsample back to full resolution with transposed convolutions (nn.ConvTranspose2d) or interpolation followed by a convolution. U-Net, designed for biomedical images, concatenates encoder features into the decoder at each resolution, recovering fine detail.

Pixel accuracy misleads when the background dominates: predicting background everywhere can score above 80%. Report each class's IoU (intersection over union of predicted and true pixels), their mean (mIoU), or the Dice coefficient, 2|A ∩ B| / (|A| + |B|).

When objects are small, cross-entropy is dominated by background pixels; class weights or a Dice loss (1 minus Dice computed from predicted probabilities) focus training on the objects, and the two losses are often combined.

Mask R-CNN adds a mask head to Faster R-CNN to output a mask for each detected object; torchvision provides it as maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2, and semantic segmentation models such as deeplabv3_resnet50.

"""Score a detector with average precision, then train a small U-Net on shape masks and measure it properly."""

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
from torchvision.ops import box_iou

from shapes import BASIC, make_shapes


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ part 1: detection

def fake_detections(n_images=60, seed=0):
    """Ground-truth boxes for one class, and a detector's imperfect output: jittered hits, misses, duplicates and
    false alarms, with confidence scores."""
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    gts, preds, scores = [], [], []
    for _ in range(n_images):
        k = int(torch.randint(1, 4, (1,), generator=g))
        xy = torch.rand(k, 2, generator=g) * 80
        wh = 10 + torch.rand(k, 2, generator=g) * 20
        gt = torch.cat([xy, xy + wh], dim=1)
        p, s = [], []
        for box in gt:
            if torch.rand(1, generator=g) < 0.85:                                   # found it, roughly
                jitter = (torch.rand(4, generator=g) - 0.5) * 0.4 * wh.mean()
                p.append(box + jitter)
                s.append(0.5 + 0.5 * torch.rand(1, generator=g))
                if torch.rand(1, generator=g) < 0.2:                                # and a duplicate
                    p.append(box + (torch.rand(4, generator=g) - 0.5) * 6)
                    s.append(0.3 + 0.4 * torch.rand(1, generator=g))
        for _ in range(int(torch.randint(0, 2, (1,), generator=g))):                 # a false alarm
            xy0 = torch.rand(2, generator=g) * 80
            p.append(torch.cat([xy0, xy0 + 15]))
            s.append(0.6 * torch.rand(1, generator=g))
        gts.append(gt)
        preds.append(torch.stack(p) if p else torch.zeros(0, 4))
        scores.append(torch.cat(s) if s else torch.zeros(0))
    return gts, preds, scores


def average_precision(gts, preds, scores, iou_threshold=0.5):
    """All-point interpolated AP for one class over many images."""
    order = sorted(((float(s), i, j) for i, sc in enumerate(scores) for j, s in enumerate(sc)), reverse=True)
    matched = [torch.zeros(len(g), dtype=torch.bool) for g in gts]
    tp = []
    for _, i, j in order:
        # TODO: compute the IoU of detection j in image i with that image's ground truths (box_iou), ignore the
        #  ground truths already matched (set their IoU to -1), and take the best. If it reaches iou_threshold,
        #  mark that ground truth matched and append 1 (a true positive); otherwise append 0 (a false positive)
        tp.append(0.0)
    tp = torch.tensor(tp)
    n_gt = sum(len(g) for g in gts)
    recall = tp.cumsum(0) / n_gt
    precision = tp.cumsum(0) / torch.arange(1, len(tp) + 1)
    # make precision monotonically decreasing from the right, then sum precision over each step in recall
    precision = torch.flip(torch.cummax(torch.flip(precision, [0]), 0).values, [0])
    steps = torch.diff(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1), recall]))
    return float((steps * precision).sum()), float(recall[-1]) if len(recall) else 0.0


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ part 2: segmentation

def block(c_in, c_out):
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU(),
                         nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU())


class MiniUNet(nn.Module):
    """32 x 32 -> 16 -> 8 and back up, with skip connections; outputs (N, n_classes, 32, 32) logits."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc1, self.enc2, self.mid = block(3, 16), block(16, 32), block(32, 64)
        self.up2, self.dec2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, 2, stride=2), block(64, 32)
        self.up1, self.dec1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 16, 2, stride=2), block(32, 16)
        self.head = nn.Conv2d(16, n_classes, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        e1 = self.enc1(x)                          # (N, 16, 32, 32)
        e2 = self.enc2(F.max_pool2d(e1, 2))        # (N, 32, 16, 16)
        m = self.mid(F.max_pool2d(e2, 2))          # (N, 64, 8, 8)
        # TODO: upsample m with up2, concatenate it with e2 along the channels and apply dec2; then upsample with
        #  up1, concatenate with e1, apply dec1, and return head(...)
        return self.head(F.interpolate(m[:, :16], scale_factor=4))


def segmentation_scores(pred, target, n_classes):
    """Pixel accuracy, and IoU and Dice for each class, from integer masks of the same shape."""
    pixel_acc = (pred == target).float().mean().item()
    ious, dices = [], []
    for c in range(n_classes):
        p, t = pred == c, target == c
        inter, union = (p & t).sum().item(), (p | t).sum().item()
        # TODO: IoU = intersection / union; Dice = 2 * intersection / (|p| + |t|), where |p| and |t| are pixel counts
        ious.append(0.0)
        dices.append(0.0)
    return pixel_acc, ious, dices


def report(name, pred, target, names):
    acc, ious, dices = segmentation_scores(pred, target, len(names))
    shapes_iou = sum(ious[1:]) / (len(ious) - 1)
    print(f"{name:22} pixel acc {acc:.3f} | IoU " + " ".join(f"{n} {v:.3f}" for n, v in zip(names, ious)) +
          f" | mIoU (shapes) {shapes_iou:.3f} | Dice (shapes) {sum(dices[1:]) / (len(dices) - 1):.3f}")


def main():
    print("== 1. Average precision")
    gts, preds, scores = fake_detections()
    print(f"{sum(len(g) for g in gts)} ground-truth boxes, {sum(len(p) for p in preds)} detections")
    for t in (0.5, 0.75):
        ap, rec = average_precision(gts, preds, scores, t)
        print(f"AP at IoU {t}: {ap:.3f} (final recall {rec:.3f})")
    coco = sum(average_precision(gts, preds, scores, t / 100)[0] for t in range(50, 100, 5)) / 10
    print(f"AP averaged over IoU 0.50:0.95: {coco:.3f}")

    print("== 2. Segmentation")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    train, test = make_shapes(1500, seed=0, setting="field"), make_shapes(300, seed=1, setting="field")
    names = ["background"] + BASIC
    model = MiniUNet(len(names))
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    for epoch in range(1, 7):
        model.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(train["masks"]), generator=g)
        for start in range(0, len(order), 32):
            idx = order[start:start + 32]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model(train["images"][idx]), train["masks"][idx])   # (N, C, H, W) vs (N, H, W)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
        print(f"epoch {epoch}  last batch loss {loss.item():.3f}")
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred = model(test["images"]).argmax(dim=1)
    report("all background", torch.zeros_like(test["masks"]), test["masks"], names)
    report("MiniUNet", pred, test["masks"], names)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Detections must be matched in order of decreasing confidence; average_precision() sorts them before the loop, so don't reorder inside it.
If the U-Net raises a shape error at torch.cat, check that you upsample before concatenating: e2 is 16 x 16 and m is 8 x 8.
Class 0 in the masks is background; the shape mIoU averages classes 1 to 3 only.

project.title: Diagnose leaf disease from field photos
project.brief: make_leaves.py generates synthetic 64 x 64 leaf photos in ImageFolder layout, in four classes: healthy, leaf_spot, blight and mosaic. train, val and test hold studio photos (one centred leaf on a plain light background in even light: 1,600, 400 and 400 images); field holds 400 photos like the ones farmers take (soil and grass behind the leaf, any angle and size, uneven light, blur, noise) for the final evaluation only, and field_val 100 more for choosing between models. Train only on studio photos and make the classifier work in the field. On the course's machine a small ResNet-style network trained without augmentation scored 0.998 on the studio test set and about 0.27 in the field, calling almost every leaf blight; geometric and photometric augmentation raised field accuracy to about 0.54, with almost no healthy field leaves recognised. Close the gap with what the course teaches: augmentation that simulates the field's backgrounds (for example, cut each studio leaf out of its plain background by colour and paste it onto random textures), stronger photometric changes, a better architecture, and optionally an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 (about 45 MB to download) with its own preprocessing. Evaluate honestly, and report what still fails.

"""Generate the capstone's synthetic leaf photos in ImageFolder layout. No downloads; about 25 MB of PNG files.

leaves/train, leaves/val and leaves/test hold "studio" photos: one leaf, centred, on a plain light background in
even light. leaves/field (400 images, for the final evaluation only) and leaves/field_val (100 images, for choosing
between models) hold photos like the ones farmers would take: soil and grass behind the leaf, any angle and size,
uneven light, blur and noise. Four classes: healthy, leaf_spot (small dark spots with yellow halos), blight
(large brown patches) and mosaic (yellow-green mottling). The same seed always gives the same files.
"""

import argparse
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter

SIZE = 64
CLASSES = ["healthy", "leaf_spot", "blight", "mosaic"]
SPLITS = {"train": ("studio", 400), "val": ("studio", 100), "test": ("studio", 100), "field": ("field", 100),
          "field_val": ("field", 25)}


def smooth_noise(rng, cells):
    """Random values on a coarse grid, bilinearly interpolated to SIZE x SIZE, scaled to 0-1."""
    grid = rng.random((cells + 1, cells + 1))
    t = np.linspace(0, cells, SIZE)
    i = np.minimum(t.astype(int), cells - 1)
    f = t - i
    rows = grid[i] * (1 - f)[:, None] + grid[i + 1] * f[:, None]
    out = rows[:, i] * (1 - f)[None, :] + rows[:, i + 1] * f[None, :]
    return (out - out.min()) / (out.max() - out.min() + 1e-9)


def leaf_photo(kind, setting, rng):
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:SIZE, 0:SIZE] + 0.5
    field = setting == "field"
    if field:   # soil and grass, in patches
        soil = np.array([0.40, 0.30, 0.20]) + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, 3)
        grass = np.array([0.25, 0.45, 0.15]) + rng.uniform(-0.08, 0.08, 3)
        mix = smooth_noise(rng, 4)[..., None]
        img = soil * (1 - mix) + grass * mix + 0.08 * (smooth_noise(rng, 16)[..., None] - 0.5)
    else:
        img = np.ones((SIZE, SIZE, 3)) * rng.uniform(0.80, 0.92)
    length = rng.uniform(18, 30) if field else rng.uniform(25, 28)
    width = length * rng.uniform(0.42, 0.55)
    cx, cy = (rng.uniform(20, 44, 2) if field else SIZE / 2 + rng.uniform(-1.5, 1.5, 2))
    angle = rng.uniform(0, np.pi) if field else rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2)
    c, s = np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)
    u, v = (c * (xx - cx) + s * (yy - cy)) / length, (-s * (xx - cx) + c * (yy - cy)) / width
    leaf = u ** 2 + (v / (1 - 0.35 * u)) ** 2 <= 1          # an egg shape, wider at the base
    green = np.array([0.20, 0.55, 0.18]) + rng.uniform(-0.05, 0.05, 3)
    shade = 0.9 + 0.2 * smooth_noise(rng, 6)[..., None]
    colour = green * shade
    vein = (np.abs(v) < 0.06) | ((np.abs(v - 0.45 * np.abs(np.sin(6 * u))) < 0.04) & (np.abs(u) < 0.8))
    colour = np.where(vein[..., None], colour * 1.25, colour)
    if kind == "leaf_spot":
        for _ in range(rng.integers(5, 11)):
            k = rng.integers(len(xx[leaf]))
            sx, sy, r = xx[leaf][k], yy[leaf][k], rng.uniform(1.4, 2.6)
            d = np.hypot(xx - sx, yy - sy)
            colour = np.where((d < r * 1.9)[..., None], np.array([0.75, 0.70, 0.20]), colour)   # yellow halo
            colour = np.where((d < r)[..., None], np.array([0.30, 0.18, 0.08]), colour)        # dark centre
    elif kind == "blight":
        patch = np.zeros((SIZE, SIZE), dtype=bool)
        for _ in range(rng.integers(1, 3)):
            ang = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
            ex, ey = cx + 0.8 * length * np.cos(ang) * 0.9, cy + 0.8 * width * np.sin(ang) * 0.9
            for _ in range(rng.integers(3, 6)):
                bx, by = ex + rng.normal(0, 4), ey + rng.normal(0, 4)
                patch |= np.hypot(xx - bx, yy - by) < rng.uniform(4, 8)
        rim = patch & ~(np.hypot(*np.gradient(patch.astype(float))) == 0)
        colour = np.where(patch[..., None], np.array([0.45, 0.30, 0.15]) * (0.85 + 0.3 * smooth_noise(rng, 8)[..., None]), colour)
        colour = np.where(rim[..., None], np.array([0.25, 0.15, 0.07]), colour)
    elif kind == "mosaic":
        mottle = smooth_noise(rng, rng.integers(5, 9)) > rng.uniform(0.5, 0.6)
        colour = np.where(mottle[..., None], np.array([0.70, 0.75, 0.25]) * shade, colour)
    img = np.where(leaf[..., None], colour, img)
    if field:   # light falling off across the frame, then noise and sometimes blur
        t = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
        img = img * (1 + rng.uniform(-0.35, 0.35) * (np.cos(t) * (xx / SIZE - 0.5) + np.sin(t) * (yy / SIZE - 0.5)))[..., None] * rng.uniform(0.75, 1.15)
    img = img + rng.normal(0, 0.04 if field else 0.015, img.shape)
    photo = Image.fromarray((np.clip(img, 0, 1) * 255).astype(np.uint8))
    if field and rng.random() < 0.5:
        photo = photo.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(rng.uniform(0.5, 1.2)))
    return photo


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="leaves")
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=7)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(args.seed)
    for split, (setting, per_class) in SPLITS.items():
        for kind in CLASSES:
            folder = Path(args.out) / split / kind
            folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            for i in range(per_class):
                leaf_photo(kind, setting, rng).save(folder / f"{kind}_{i:04d}.png")
        print(f"{split:6} {setting:7} {per_class * len(CLASSES)} images")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
